Affine surfaces
with trivial Makar-Limanov invariantThanks: Research supported by a grant from NSERC Canada.

Daniel Daigle Address: Department of Mathematics and Statistics

Ottawa, Canada K1N 6N5 Email address: ddaigle@uottawa.ca
Abstract.

We study the class of 22-dimensional affine 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-domains RR satisfying ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}, where 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is an arbitrary field of characteristic zero. In particular, we obtain the following result: Let RR be a localization of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a field of characteristic zero. If ML⁡(R)=K\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)=K for some field K⊂RK\subset R such that trdegK⁡R=2\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{K}R=2, then RR is KK-isomorphic to K⁡[X,Y,Z]/(X​Y−P⁡(Z))K[X,Y,Z]/(XY-P(Z)) for some nonconstant P⁡(Z)∈K⁡[Z]P(Z)\in K[Z].

Key words and phrases: 
Locally nilpotent derivations, group actions, Danielewski surfaces, affine surfaces, Makar-Limanov invariant, absolute constants

1. Introduction

Let us recall the definition of the Makar-Limanov invariant:

1.1 Definition.

If RR is a ring of characteristic zero, a derivation D:R→RD:R\to R is said to be locally nilpotent if for each r∈Rr\in R there exists n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} (depending on rr) such that Dn​(r)=0D^{n}(r)=0. We use the following notations:

lnd⁡(R)\displaystyle\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R) =set of locally nilpotent derivations D:R→R\displaystyle=\textrm{set of locally nilpotent derivations $D:R\to R$}
klnd⁡(R)\displaystyle\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(R) ={ker⁡D∣D∈lnd⁡(R)​ and ​D≠0}\displaystyle=\big\{\,\ker D\,\mid\,D\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R)\text{ and }D\neq 0\,\big\}
ML⁡(R)\displaystyle\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R) =⋂D∈lnd​(R)ker⁡(D).\displaystyle=\bigcap_{D\in\text{\sc lnd}(R)}\ker(D).

We are interested in the class of 22-dimensional affine 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-domains RR satisfying ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}, where 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is a field of characteristic zero. The corresponding class of affine algebraic surfaces was studied by several authors ([1], [2], [7], [8], [9], [14], [17], in particular), but almost always under the assumption that 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is algebraically closed, or even 𝐤=ℂ{\rm\bf k}=\mathbb{C}. In this paper we obtain some partial results valid when 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is an arbitrary field of characteristic zero. We are particularly interested in the following subclass:

1.2 Definition.

Given a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} of characteristic zero, let 𝔇⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) be the class of 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebras isomorphic to 𝐤⁡[X,Y,Z]/(X​Y−φ⁡(Z)){\rm\bf k}[X,Y,Z]/(XY-\varphi(Z)) for some nonconstant polynomial in one variable φ⁡(Z)∈𝐤⁡[Z]∖𝐤\varphi(Z)\in{\rm\bf k}[Z]\setminus{\rm\bf k}, where X,Y,ZX,Y,Z are indeterminates over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}.

The class 𝔇⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) was studied in [4], [5] and [16], in particular. It is well-known that if R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) then RR is a 22-dimensional normal affine domain satisfying ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}. It is also known that the converse is not true, which raises the following:

Question.

Suppose that RR is a 22-dimensional affine 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-domain with ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}. Under what additional assumptions can we infer that R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k})?

Section 3 completely answers this question in the case where RR is a smooth 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra. This is achieved by reducing to the case 𝐤=ℂ{\rm\bf k}=\mathbb{C}, which was solved by Bandman and Makar-Limanov. This reduction is non-trivial, and makes essential use of the main result of Section 2. Also note Corollary 3.8, which gives a pleasant answer to the above question in the factorial case. Then we derive several consequences from Section 3, for instance consider the following special case of Theorem 4.1:

Let RR be a localization of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over a field of characteristic zero. If ML⁡(R)=K\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)=K for some field K⊂RK\subset R such that trdegK⁡R=2\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{K}R=2, then R∈𝔇⁡(K)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K).

In turn, this has consequences in the study of GaG_{a}-actions on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Conventions.

All rings and algebras are commutative, associative and unital. If AA is a ring, we write A∗A^{*} for the units of AA; if AA is a domain, Frac⁡A\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}A is its field of fractions. If A⊆BA\subseteq B are rings, “ B=A[n]B=A^{[n]} ” means that BB is AA-isomorphic to the polynomial algebra in nn variables over AA. If L/KL/K is a field extension, “ L=K(n)L=K^{(n)} ” means that LL is a purely transcendental extension of KK and trdegK⁡L=n\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{K}L=n (transcendence degree).

In [5], one defines a Danielewski surface to be a pair (R,𝐤)(R,{\rm\bf k}) such that R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}). In the present paper we avoid using the term “Danielewski surface” in that sense, because it is incompatible with accepted usage. The reader should keep this in mind when consulting [5] (our main reference for Section 2).

2. Base extension

Let 𝐤{\rm\bf k} be a field of characteristic zero. It is clear that if R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) then K⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(K)K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) for every field extension K/𝐤K/{\rm\bf k}. However, if K⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(K)K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) for some KK, it does not follow that R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) (see Example 2.2, below).

2.1 Remark.

If R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) then Spec⁡R\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}R has infinitely many 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-rational points. (Indeed, if R=𝐤⁡[X,Y,Z]/(X​Y−φ⁡(Z))R={\rm\bf k}[X,Y,Z]/(XY-\varphi(Z)) then there is a bijection between the set of 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-rational points of Spec⁡R\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}R and the zero-set in 𝐤3{\rm\bf k}^{3} of the polynomial X​Y−φ⁡(Z)XY-\varphi(Z).)

2.2 Example.

Let A=ℝ⁡[X,Y,Z]/(f)A=\mathbb{R}[X,Y,Z]/(f), where f=X2+Y2+Z2f=X^{2}+Y^{2}+Z^{2}. Viewing ff as an element of ℂ⁡[X,Y,Z]\mathbb{C}[X,Y,Z] we have f=(X+i​Y)​(X−i​Y)+Z2f=(X+iY)(X-iY)+Z^{2} (where i2=−1i^{2}=-1), so ℂ⊗ℝA≅ℂ⁡[U,V,W]/(U​V+W2)∈𝔇⁡(ℂ)\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}A\cong\mathbb{C}[U,V,W]/(UV+W^{2})\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(\mathbb{C}). As Spec⁡A\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}A has only one ℝ\mathbb{R}-rational point, A∉𝔇⁡(ℝ)A\notin\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(\mathbb{R}) by Remark 2.1. Thus

A∉𝔇⁡(ℝ)A\notin\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(\mathbb{R}) and ℂ⊗ℝA∈𝔇⁡(ℂ)\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}A\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(\mathbb{C}).

Moreover, if we define A′=ℝ⁡[U,V,W]/(U​V+W2)∈𝔇⁡(ℝ)A^{\prime}=\mathbb{R}[U,V,W]/(UV+W^{2})\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(\mathbb{R}) then A≇A′A\not\cong A^{\prime} but ℂ⊗ℝA≅ℂ⊗ℝA′\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}A\cong\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\mathbb{R}}A^{\prime}.

2.3 Theorem.

For an algebra RR over a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} of characteristic zero, the following conditions are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k})

  2. (b)

    ML⁡(R)≠R\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)\neq R and there exists a field extension K/𝐤K/{\rm\bf k} such that K⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(K)K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K).

We shall prove this after some preparation.

2.4 Some facts.

Refer to [11] or [13] for background on locally nilpotent derivations. Statement (c) is due to Rentschler [20] and (d) to Nouazé and Gabriel [19] and Wright [21].

  1. (a)

    If A∈klnd⁡(B)A\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B) where BB is a domain of characteristic zero then AA is factorially closed in BB (i.e., if x,y∈B∖{0}x,y\in B\setminus\{0\} and x​y∈Axy\in A then x,y∈Ax,y\in A). It follows that ML⁡(B)\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(B) is factorially closed in BB. Any factorially closed subring AA of BB is in particular algebraically closed in BB (i.e., if x∈Bx\in B is a root of a nonzero polynomial with coefficients in AA then x∈Ax\in A) and satisfies A∗=B∗A^{*}=B^{*} (in particular, any field contained in BB is contained in AA).

  2. (b)

    Let BB be a noetherian domain of characteristic zero. If 0≠D∈lnd⁡(B)0\neq D\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(B) then D=α​D0D=\alpha D_{0} for some α∈ker⁡(D)\alpha\in\ker(D) and D0∈lnd⁡(B)D_{0}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(B) where D0D_{0} is irreducible (i.e., the only principal ideal of BB which contains D0​(B)D_{0}(B) is BB).

  3. (c)

    Let B=𝐤[2]B={\rm\bf k}^{[2]} where 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is a field of characteristic zero. If D∈lnd⁡(B)D\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(B) is irreducible then there exist X,YX,Y such that B=𝐤⁡[X,Y]B={\rm\bf k}[X,Y] and D=∂/∂YD=\partial/\partial Y.

  4. (d)

    Let BB be a ℚ\mathbb{Q}-algebra. If D∈lnd⁡(B)D\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(B) and s∈Bs\in B satisfy D​s∈B∗Ds\in B^{*} then B=A⁡[s]=A[1]B=A[s]=A^{[1]} where A=ker⁡DA=\ker D.

2.5 Lemma.

Let 𝐤{\rm\bf k} be a field of characteristic zero and RR a 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra satisfying:

there exists a field extension 𝐤¯/𝐤{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}/{\rm\bf k} such that 𝐤¯⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤¯){\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}).

Then RR is a two-dimensional normal affine domain over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} and R∗=𝐤∗R^{*}={\rm\bf k}^{*}.

Proof.

This is rather simple but it will be convenient to refer to this proof later. Choose a field extension 𝐤¯/𝐤{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}/{\rm\bf k} such that 𝐤¯⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤¯){\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}) and let R¯=𝐤¯⊗𝐤R\bar{R}={\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R. As RR is a flat 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-module, the canonical homomorphism 𝐤⊗𝐤R→𝐤¯⊗𝐤R{\rm\bf k}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\to{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R is injective, so we may regard RR as a subring of R¯\bar{R}. In particular, RR is an integral domain and we have the diagram:

where S=R∖{0}S=R\setminus\{0\}. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a basis of 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}} over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} such that 1∈ℬ1\in\mathcal{B}. Note that ℬ\mathcal{B} is also a basis of the free RR-module R¯\bar{R} and of the vector space S−1​R¯S^{-1}\bar{R} over Frac⁡R\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}R. It follows:

(1) 𝐤¯∩R=𝐤andR¯∩Frac⁡R=R.{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\cap R={\rm\bf k}\quad\textit{and}\quad\bar{R}\cap\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}R=R.

As R¯∈𝔇⁡(𝐤¯)\bar{R}\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}), [5, 2.3] implies that R¯∗=𝐤¯∗\bar{R}^{*}={\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}^{*} and that R¯\bar{R} is a normal domain; so (1) implies that R∗=𝐤∗R^{*}={\rm\bf k}^{*} and that RR is a normal domain. Also:

(2) If EE is a subset of RR such that 𝐤¯​[E]=R¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}[E]=\bar{R}, then 𝐤⁡[E]=R{\rm\bf k}[E]=R.

Indeed, ℬ\mathcal{B} is a basis of the RR-module R¯\bar{R} and a spanning set of the 𝐤⁡[E]{\rm\bf k}[E]-module R¯\bar{R}; as 𝐤⁡[E]⊆R{\rm\bf k}[E]\subseteq R, it follows that 𝐤⁡[E]=R{\rm\bf k}[E]=R.

Note that RR is affine over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}, by (2) and the fact that R¯\bar{R} is affine over 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}. Let n=dimRn=\dim R then, by Noether Normalization Lemma, there exists a subalgebra R0=𝐤[n]R_{0}={\rm\bf k}^{[n]} of RR over which RR is integral. Then R¯=𝐤¯⊗𝐤R\bar{R}={\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R is integral over 𝐤¯⊗𝐤R0=𝐤¯[n]{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R_{0}={\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}^{[n]}, so n=dimR¯=2n=\dim\bar{R}=2. ∎

We borrow the following notation from [5, 2.1].

Given a 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra RR, let Γ𝐤​(R)\Gamma_{\rm\bf k}(R) denote the (possibly empty) set of ordered triples (x1,x2,y)∈R×R×R(x_{1},x_{2},y)\in R\times R\times R satisfying:

Proof of Theorem 2.3.

That R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) implies ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k} is well-known (for instance it follows from part (d) of [5, 2.3]), so it suffices to prove that (b) implies (a).

Suppose that RR satisfies (b). Note that if K/𝐤K/{\rm\bf k} is a field extension satisfying K⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(K)K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) then for any field extension L/KL/K we have L⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(L)L\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(L). In particular, there exists a field extension 𝐤¯/𝐤{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}/{\rm\bf k} such that 𝐤¯⊗𝐤R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤¯){\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}) and such that 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}} is an algebraically closed field. We fix such a field 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}. The fact that 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}} is algebraically closed implies that

Thus, for c∈𝐤¯c\in{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}},

R¯/(f−c)​R¯≅𝐤¯​[X1,X2,Y]/(X1−(c−λ),X1​X2−P⁡(Y))\bar{R}/(f-c)\bar{R}\ \cong\ {\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}[X_{1},X_{2},Y]/(X_{1}-(c-\lambda),\ X_{1}X_{2}-P(Y))

is a domain if and only if c≠λc\neq\lambda. This proves (7).

Let θ∈Gal⁡(𝐤¯/𝐤)\theta\in\operatorname{{\rm Gal}}({\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}/{\rm\bf k}). Then θ\theta extends to some Θ∈AutR⁡(R¯)\Theta\in\operatorname{{\rm Aut}}_{R}(\bar{R}) and Θ\Theta determines a ring isomorphism

So R¯/(f−θ⁡(λ))​R¯\bar{R}/(f-\theta(\lambda))\bar{R} is not a domain and it follows from (7) that θ⁡(λ)=λ\theta(\lambda)=\lambda. As this holds for every θ∈Gal⁡(𝐤¯/𝐤)\theta\in\operatorname{{\rm Gal}}({\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}/{\rm\bf k}), (3) implies that λ∈𝐤\lambda\in{\rm\bf k}. To summarize, if we define x1=f−λx_{1}=f-\lambda then

x1,s∈Rx_{1},s\in R and there exists x2∈R¯x_{2}\in\bar{R} such that (x1,x2,s)∈Γ𝐤¯​(R¯)(x_{1},x_{2},s)\in\Gamma_{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}(\bar{R}).

Then ∑λ∈ℬ(x1​Gλ)​λ=Φ⁡(s)=∑λ∈ℬΦλ​(s)​λ\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{B}}(x_{1}G_{\lambda})\lambda=\Phi(s)=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{B}}\Phi_{\lambda}(s)\lambda, so for every λ∈ℬ\lambda\in\mathcal{B} we have Φλ​(s)=x1​Gλ\Phi_{\lambda}(s)=x_{1}G_{\lambda}, i.e., Φλ​(s)∈J=φ⁡(s)​𝐤​[s]\Phi_{\lambda}(s)\in J=\varphi(s){\rm\bf k}[s]. J¯=φ⁡(s)​𝐤¯​[s].\bar{J}=\varphi(s){\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}[s].

3. On a result of Bandman and Makar-Limanov

In this paper we adopt the following:

3.1 Definition.

Let RR be an affine algebra over a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} and let q=dimRq=\dim R. We say that RR is a complete intersection over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} if R≅𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xp+q]/(f1,…,fp)R\cong{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{p}) for some p≥0p\geq 0 and some f1,…,fp∈𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xp+q]f_{1},\dots,f_{p}\in{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}].

We refer to [18, 28.D] for the definition of a smooth 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra and to [18, 26.C] for the definition of the RR-module ΩR/𝐤\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}} (the module of differentials of RR over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}), where RR is a 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra.

3.2 Theorem.

Let 𝐤{\rm\bf k} be a field of characteristic zero and RR a smooth affine 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-domain of dimension 22 such that ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}. Then the following are equivalent:

  1. (a)

    R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k})

  2. (b)

    RR is generated by 33 elements as a 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra

  3. (c)

    RR is a complete intersection over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}

  4. (d)

    ⋀2ΩR/𝐤≅R\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}}\cong R.

We shall prove this by reducing to the case 𝐤=ℂ{\rm\bf k}=\mathbb{C}, which was proved by Bandman and Makar-Limanov in [1]. That reduction makes essential use of Theorem 2.3.

3.3 Remark.

Let 𝐤{\rm\bf k} be a field of characteristic zero. According to the definition of “Danielewski surface over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}” given in [10], one has the following situation:

where danml⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc danml}}({\rm\bf k}) is the class of Danielewski surfaces SS over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} satisfying ML⁡(S)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(S)={\rm\bf k}, sml⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc sml}}({\rm\bf k}) is the larger class of smooth affine surfaces SS over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} satisfying ML⁡(S)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(S)={\rm\bf k}, and 𝔇⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) is the class of surfaces corresponding to the already defined class 𝔇⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}) of 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebras. Among other things, paper [10] classifies the elements of danml⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc danml}}({\rm\bf k}) and characterizes those which belong to 𝔇⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}). In contrast, Theorem 3.2 characterizes the elements of sml⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc sml}}({\rm\bf k}) which belong to 𝔇⁡(𝐤)\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}).

3.4 Remark.

Let RR be a qq-dimensional smooth affine domain over a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} of characteristic zero. Then X=Spec⁡RX=\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}R is in particular an irreducible regular scheme of finite type over the perfect field 𝐤{\rm\bf k}; so, by [15, ex. 8.1(c), p. 187], the sheaf of differentials ΩX/𝐤\Omega_{X/{\rm\bf k}} is locally free of rank qq; so the canonical sheaf ωX=⋀qΩX/𝐤\omega_{X}=\bigwedge^{q}\Omega_{X/{\rm\bf k}} is locally free of rank 11, i.e., is an invertible sheaf on XX. As ωX\omega_{X} and the structure sheaf 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X} are respectively the sheaves associated to the RR-modules ⋀qΩR/𝐤\bigwedge^{q}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}} and RR, the condition ⋀qΩR/𝐤≅R\bigwedge^{q}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}}\cong R is equivalent to ωX≅𝒪X\omega_{X}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X} (one says that XX has trivial canonical sheaf). This is also equivalent to the canonical divisor of XX being linearly equivalent to zero (because Pic⁡(X)≅Cl⁡(X)\operatorname{{\rm Pic}}(X)\cong\operatorname{{\rm Cl}}(X) by [15, 6.16 p. 145]).

3.5 Remark.

Let A′A^{\prime} and BB be algebras over a ring AA and let B′=A′⊗ABB^{\prime}=A^{\prime}\otimes_{A}B. Then ΩB′/A′≅B′⊗BΩB/A\Omega_{B^{\prime}/A^{\prime}}\cong B^{\prime}\otimes_{B}\Omega_{B/A} (cf. [18, p. 186]) and, for any BB-module MM, ⋀n(B′⊗BM)≅B′⊗⋀nB⁡M\bigwedge^{n}(B^{\prime}\otimes_{B}M)\cong B^{\prime}\otimes_{B}\bigwedge^{n}M for every nn ([3], Chap. 3, § 7, No 5, Prop. 8). Consequently, ⋀nΩB′/A′≅B′⊗⋀nB⁡ΩB/A\bigwedge^{n}\Omega_{B^{\prime}/A^{\prime}}\cong B^{\prime}\otimes_{B}\bigwedge^{n}\Omega_{B/A}.

3.6 Lemma.

Let RR be an algebra over a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k}. If RR is a complete intersection over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} and a smooth 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra, then ⋀qΩR/𝐤≅R\bigwedge^{q}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}}\cong R where q=dimRq=\dim R.

This is the well-known fact that a smooth complete intersection has trivial canonical sheaf, but we don’t know a suitable reference so we sketch a proof.

Proof of 3.6.

Let R=𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xp+q]/(f1,…,fp)R={\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{p}) and let φi​j∈R\varphi_{ij}\in R be the image of ∂fj∂Xi\frac{\partial f_{j}}{\partial X_{i}}. Because RR is smooth over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}, [18, 29.E] implies that the matrix (φi​j)(\varphi_{ij}) satisfies:

(8) the p×pp\times p determinants of (φi​j)(\varphi_{ij}) generate the unit ideal of RR.

By [15, 8.4A, p. 173], there is an exact sequence Rp→𝜑Rp+q→ΩR/𝐤→0R^{p}\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }R^{p+q}\to\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}}\to 0 of RR-linear maps where φ\varphi is the map corresponding to the matrix (φi​j)(\varphi_{ij}). Now if RR is a ring and Rp→𝜑Rp+q→M→0R^{p}\xrightarrow{\ \varphi\ }R^{p+q}\to M\to 0 is an exact sequence of RR-linear maps such that φ\varphi satisfies (8), then ⋀qM≅R\bigwedge^{q}M\cong R. ∎

3.7 Lemma.

Let RR be an integral domain containing a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} of characteristic zero. If RR is normal and ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}, then for any field extension KK of 𝐤{\rm\bf k} we have:

  1. (a)

    K⊗𝐤RK\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R is an integral domain

  2. (b)

    ML⁡(K⊗𝐤R)=K\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R)=K.

Proof.

As 𝐤=ML⁡(R){\rm\bf k}=\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R) is algebraically closed in RR (2.4(a)) and RR is normal, it follows that 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is algebraically closed in L=Frac⁡RL=\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}R. By [22, Cor. 2, p. 198], K⊗𝐤LK\otimes_{\rm\bf k}L is an integral domain. As KK is flat over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} and R→LR\to L is injective, K⊗𝐤R→K⊗𝐤LK\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R\to K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}L is injective and (a) is proved.

Let ξ∈ML⁡(K⊗𝐤R)\xi\in\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R). Consider a basis ℬ\mathcal{B} of KK over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}; note that ℬ\mathcal{B} is also a basis of the free RR-module R′=K⊗𝐤RR^{\prime}=K\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R and write ξ=∑λ∈ℬxλ​λ\xi=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{B}}x_{\lambda}\lambda (where xλ∈Rx_{\lambda}\in R). If D∈lnd⁡(R)D\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R) then DD extends to an element D′∈lnd⁡(R′)D^{\prime}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R^{\prime}) and the equation 0=D′​(ξ)=∑λ∈ℬD⁡(xλ)​λ0=D^{\prime}(\xi)=\sum_{\lambda\in\mathcal{B}}D(x_{\lambda})\lambda shows that D⁡(xλ)=0D(x_{\lambda})=0 for all λ∈ℬ\lambda\in\mathcal{B}. As this holds for every D∈lnd⁡(R)D\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R), we have xλ∈ML⁡(R)=𝐤x_{\lambda}\in\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k} for all λ\lambda, so ξ∈K\xi\in K. ∎

Proof of Theorem 3.2.

Implications (a)⇒(b)⇒(c)\text{(a)}\Rightarrow\text{(b)}\Rightarrow\text{(c)} are trivial and (c)⇒(d)\text{(c)}\Rightarrow\text{(d)} is Lemma 3.6, so only (d)⇒(a)\text{(d)}\Rightarrow\text{(a)} requires a proof. Assume for a moment that 𝐤=ℂ{\rm\bf k}=\mathbb{C} and suppose that RR satisfies (d). Then Lemmas 4 and 5 of [1] imply that R∈𝔇⁡(ℂ)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(\mathbb{C}), so the Theorem is valid in the case 𝐤=ℂ{\rm\bf k}=\mathbb{C}.

Let 𝐤{\rm\bf k} be a field of characteristic zero, consider a smooth affine 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-domain RR of dimension 22 such that ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}, and suppose that RR satisfies (d).

We have R≅𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xn]/(f1,…,fm)R\cong{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) for some m,n≥0m,n\geq 0 and some f1,…,fm∈𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xn]f_{1},\dots,f_{m}\in{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]. Also consider D1,D2∈lnd⁡(R)D_{1},D_{2}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R) such that ker⁡D1∩ker⁡D2=𝐤\ker D_{1}\cap\ker D_{2}={\rm\bf k}. Each DiD_{i} can be lifted to a (not necessarely locally nilpotent) 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-derivation δi\delta_{i} of 𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xn]{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]. Let 𝐤0{\rm\bf k}_{0} be a subfield of 𝐤{\rm\bf k} which is finitely generated over ℚ\mathbb{Q} and which contains all coefficients of the polynomials fif_{i} and δi​(Xj)\delta_{i}(X_{j}). Define R0=𝐤0​[X1,…,Xn]/(f1,…,fm)R_{0}={\rm\bf k}_{0}[X_{1},\dots,X_{n}]/(f_{1},\dots,f_{m}) and note that 𝐤⊗𝐤0R0≅R{\rm\bf k}\otimes_{{\rm\bf k}_{0}}R_{0}\cong R. As 𝐤0→𝐤{\rm\bf k}_{0}\to{\rm\bf k} is injective and R0R_{0} is flat over 𝐤0{\rm\bf k}_{0}, 𝐤0⊗𝐤0R0→𝐤⊗𝐤0R0{\rm\bf k}_{0}\otimes_{{\rm\bf k}_{0}}R_{0}\to{\rm\bf k}\otimes_{{\rm\bf k}_{0}}R_{0} is injective and we may regard R0R_{0} as a subring of RR. In particular, R0R_{0} is a domain (a 22-dimensional affine 𝐤0{\rm\bf k}_{0}-domain). Also note that Di​(R0)⊆R0D_{i}(R_{0})\subseteq R_{0} for i=1,2i=1,2; if di:R0→R0d_{i}:R_{0}\to R_{0} is the restriction of DiD_{i} then d1,d2∈lnd⁡(R0)d_{1},d_{2}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(R_{0}) and ker⁡d1∩ker⁡d2=𝐤∩R0=𝐤0\ker d_{1}\cap\ker d_{2}={\rm\bf k}\cap R_{0}={\rm\bf k}_{0} (see (1) for the last equality), showing that ML⁡(R0)=𝐤0\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R_{0})={\rm\bf k}_{0}. As 𝐤0{\rm\bf k}_{0} is a field and 𝐤→R{\rm\bf k}\to R is obtained from 𝐤0→R0{\rm\bf k}_{0}\to R_{0} by base extension, the fact that 𝐤→R{\rm\bf k}\to R is smooth implies that 𝐤0→R0{\rm\bf k}_{0}\to R_{0} is smooth (cf. [18, 28.O]).

Consider the RR-module M=⋀2ΩR/𝐤M=\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}} and the R0R_{0}-module M0=⋀2ΩR0/𝐤0M_{0}=\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R_{0}/{\rm\bf k}_{0}}. Consider an isomorphism of RR-modules θ:R→M\theta:R\to M and let ω=θ⁡(1)\omega=\theta(1). We have R⊗R0M0≅MR\otimes_{R_{0}}M_{0}\cong M by 3.5, so there is a natural homomorphism M0→R⊗R0M0≅MM_{0}\to R\otimes_{R_{0}}M_{0}\cong M, x↦1⊗xx\mapsto 1\otimes x; by adjoining a finite subset of 𝐤{\rm\bf k} to 𝐤0{\rm\bf k}_{0}, we may arrange that there exists ω0∈M0\omega_{0}\in M_{0} such that 1⊗ω0=ω1\otimes\omega_{0}=\omega. Consider the R0R_{0}-linear map f:R0→M0f:R_{0}\to M_{0}, f⁡(a)=a​ω0f(a)=a\omega_{0}. Note that R=𝐤⊗𝐤0R0R={\rm\bf k}\otimes_{{\rm\bf k}_{0}}R_{0} is faithfully flat as an R0R_{0}-module and that applying the functor R⊗R0¯R\otimes_{R_{0}}\underline{\ \ } to ff yields the isomorphism θ\theta; so ff is an isomorphism, so ⋀2ΩR0/𝐤0≅R0\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R_{0}/{\rm\bf k}_{0}}\cong R_{0}. As R∈𝒟⁡(𝐤)R\in\mathcal{D}({\rm\bf k}) would follow from R0∈𝒟⁡(𝐤0)R_{0}\in\mathcal{D}({\rm\bf k}_{0}), the problem reduces to proving the case 𝐤=𝐤0{\rm\bf k}={\rm\bf k}_{0} of the theorem. Now 𝐤0{\rm\bf k}_{0} is isomorphic to a subfield of ℂ\mathbb{C}, so it suffices to prove the theorem in the case 𝐤⊆ℂ{\rm\bf k}\subseteq\mathbb{C}.

Assume that 𝐤⊆ℂ{\rm\bf k}\subseteq\mathbb{C}. As RR is smooth over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}, the local ring R𝔭R_{\mathfrak{p}} is regular for every 𝔭∈Spec⁡R{\mathfrak{p}}\in\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}R (by [18, 28.E,F,K]) so in particular RR is a normal domain. Then it follows from 3.7 that R′=ℂ⊗𝐤RR^{\prime}=\mathbb{C}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}R is an integral domain and that ML⁡(R′)=ℂ\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R^{\prime})=\mathbb{C}. By [18, 28.G], R′R^{\prime} is smooth over ℂ\mathbb{C}. It is clear that dimR′=2\dim R^{\prime}=2 (for instance see the proof of 2.5) and 3.5 gives ⋀2ΩR′/ℂ≅R′⊗⋀2R⁡ΩR/𝐤≅R′⊗RR≅R′\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R^{\prime}/\mathbb{C}}\cong R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}}\cong R^{\prime}\otimes_{R}R\cong R^{\prime}. As the Theorem is valid over ℂ\mathbb{C}, it follows that R′∈𝒟⁡(ℂ)R^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{C}). As ML⁡(R)=𝐤≠R\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}\neq R, Theorem 2.3 implies that R∈𝒟⁡(𝐤)R\in\mathcal{D}({\rm\bf k}). ∎

3.8 Corollary.

Let RR be a 22-dimensional affine domain over a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} of characteristic zero. If RR is a UFD and a smooth 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebra satisfying ML⁡(R)=𝐤\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)={\rm\bf k}, then R∈𝔇⁡(𝐤)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}({\rm\bf k}).

Proof.

Since RR is a UFD, the scheme X=Spec⁡RX=\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}R has a trivial divisor class group [15, 6.2 p. 131]. By Remark 3.4, it follows that ⋀2ΩR/𝐤≅R\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R/{\rm\bf k}}\cong R and the desired conclusion follows from Theorem 3.2. ∎

4. Localizations of nice rings

Throughout this section we fix a field 𝐤{\rm\bf k} of characteristic zero and we consider the class 𝒩⁡(𝐤)\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}) of 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebras BB satisfying the following conditions:

BB is a geometrically integral affine 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-domain which is smooth over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} and satisfies at least one of the following conditions:

  • •

    BB is a UFD; or

  • •

    BB is a complete intersection over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}.

Note that 𝐤[n]∈𝒩⁡(𝐤){\rm\bf k}^{[n]}\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}) for every nn.

4.1 Theorem.

Suppose that RR is a localization of a ring belonging to the class 𝒩⁡(𝐤)\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}). If ML⁡(R)=K\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)=K for some field K⊂RK\subset R such that trdegK⁡R=2\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{K}R=2, then R∈𝔇⁡(K)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K).

4.2 Lemma.

Let B∈𝒩⁡(𝐤)B\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}), let EE be a finitely generated 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-subalbebra of BB and let S=E∖{0}S=E\setminus\{0\}. Then S−1​BS^{-1}B is a smooth algebra over the field S−1​ES^{-1}E.

Proof.

Let 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}} be an algebraic closure of 𝐤{\rm\bf k} and define E¯=𝐤¯⊗𝐤E\bar{E}={\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}E and B¯=𝐤¯⊗𝐤B\bar{B}={\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}\otimes_{\rm\bf k}B. Note that B¯\bar{B} is a domain because BB is geometrically integral, and E¯→B¯\bar{E}\to\bar{B} is injective because 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}} is flat over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}. Let K=Frac⁡EK=\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}E and L=Frac⁡E¯L=\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}\bar{E}. As B¯\bar{B} is smooth over 𝐤¯{\bar{{\rm\bf k}}}, applying [15, 10.7, p. 272] to Spec⁡B¯→Spec⁡E¯\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}\bar{B}\to\operatorname{{\rm Spec}}\bar{E} implies that L→L⊗E¯B¯L\to L\otimes_{\bar{E}}\bar{B} is smooth. It is not difficult to see that L→L⊗E¯B¯L\to L\otimes_{\bar{E}}\bar{B} is obtained from K→K⊗EBK\to K\otimes_{E}B by base extension. As KK is a field and L→L⊗E¯B¯L\to L\otimes_{\bar{E}}\bar{B} is smooth, it follows from [18, 28.O] that K→K⊗EBK\to K\otimes_{E}B is smooth. ∎

4.3 Lemma.

Let B∈𝒩⁡(𝐤)B\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}), let SS be a multiplicative subset of BB and suppose that KK is a field such that 𝐤∪S⊆K⊆S−1​B{\rm\bf k}\cup S\subseteq K\subseteq S^{-1}B. Then S−1​BS^{-1}B is a smooth KK-algebra and some transcendence basis of K/𝐤K/{\rm\bf k} is a subset of BB.

Proof.

Note that K/𝐤K/{\rm\bf k} is a finitely generated field extension and write K=𝐤⁡(α1,…,αm)K={\rm\bf k}(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m}). For each ii we have αi=bi/si\alpha_{i}=b_{i}/s_{i} for some bi∈Bb_{i}\in B and si∈Ss_{i}\in S; as S⊆KS\subseteq K, we have bi=si​αi∈Kb_{i}=s_{i}\alpha_{i}\in K. Define E=𝐤⁡[b1,…,bm,s1,…,sm]⊆KE={\rm\bf k}[b_{1},\dots,b_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{m}]\subseteq K and S1=E∖{0}S_{1}=E\setminus\{0\}, then S1−1​E=KS_{1}^{-1}E=K and hence S1−1​B=S−1​BS_{1}^{-1}B=S^{-1}B. By Lemma 4.2, S−1​BS^{-1}B is a smooth KK-algebra. Moreover, {b1,…,bm,s1,…,sm}\{b_{1},\dots,b_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{m}\} contains a transcendence basis of K/𝐤K/{\rm\bf k}. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We have R=S−1​BR=S^{-1}B for some B∈𝒩⁡(𝐤)B\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}) and some multiplicative subset SS of BB. As 𝐤∗∪S⊆R∗⊆ML⁡(R)=K{\rm\bf k}^{*}\cup S\subseteq R^{*}\subseteq\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(R)=K, RR is smooth over KK by Lemma 4.3. By definition of 𝒩⁡(𝐤)\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}), BB is a UFD or a complete intersection over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}.

If BB is a UFD then so is RR; in this case we obtain R∈𝔇⁡(K)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) by Corollary 3.8, so we are done.

From now-on, assume that BB is a complete intersection over 𝐤{\rm\bf k}. Let q=dimBq=\dim B and write B=𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xp+q]/(G1,…,Gp)B={\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]/(G_{1},\dots,G_{p}). Using Lemma 4.3 again, choose a transcendence basis {f1,…,fq−2}\{f_{1},\dots,f_{q-2}\} of KK over 𝐤{\rm\bf k} such that f1,…,fq−2∈Bf_{1},\dots,f_{q-2}\in B; let S0=𝐤⁡[f1,…,fq−2]∖{0}S_{0}={\rm\bf k}[f_{1},\dots,f_{q-2}]\setminus\{0\} and K0=𝐤⁡(f1,…,fq−2)K_{0}={\rm\bf k}(f_{1},\dots,f_{q-2}). We claim:

(9) S0−1​BS_{0}^{-1}B is a complete intersection over K0K_{0}.

Let us prove this. For 1≤i≤q−21\leq i\leq q-2, choose Fi∈𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xp+q]F_{i}\in{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}] such that π⁡(Fi)=fi\pi(F_{i})=f_{i} where π:𝐤⁡[X1,…,Xp+q]→B\pi:{\rm\bf k}[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]\to B is the canonical epimorphism. Also, let T1,…,Tq−2T_{1},\dots,T_{q-2} be extra indeterminates. The 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-homomorphism 𝐤⁡[T1,…,Tq−2,X1,…,Xp+q]→B{\rm\bf k}[T_{1},\dots,T_{q-2},X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]\to B which maps TiT_{i} to fif_{i} and XiX_{i} to π⁡(Xi)\pi(X_{i}) has kernel (G1,…,Gp,F1−T1,…,Fq−2−Tq−2)(G_{1},\dots,G_{p},F_{1}-T_{1},\dots,F_{q-2}-T_{q-2}), so there is an isomorphism of 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebras

B≅𝐤⁡[T1,…,Tq−2,X1,…,Xp+q]/(G1,…,Gp,F1−T1,…,Fq−2−Tq−2).B\cong{\rm\bf k}[T_{1},\dots,T_{q-2},X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]/(G_{1},\dots,G_{p},F_{1}-T_{1},\dots,F_{q-2}-T_{q-2}).

Localization gives an an isomorphism of 𝐤{\rm\bf k}-algebras

(10) S0−1​B≅𝐤⁡(T1,…,Tq−2)​[X1,…,Xp+q]/(G1,…,Gp,F1−T1,…,Fq−2−Tq−2)S_{0}^{-1}B\cong{\rm\bf k}(T_{1},\dots,T_{q-2})[X_{1},\dots,X_{p+q}]/(G_{1},\dots,G_{p},F_{1}-T_{1},\dots,F_{q-2}-T_{q-2})

which maps K0K_{0} onto 𝐤⁡(T1,…,Tq−2){\rm\bf k}(T_{1},\dots,T_{q-2}). As the right hand side of (10) is a complete intersection over 𝐤⁡(T1,…,Tq−2){\rm\bf k}(T_{1},\dots,T_{q-2}), assertion (9) is proved. Then we obtain

(11) ⋀2ΩS0−1​B/K0≅S0−1​B\textstyle\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{S_{0}^{-1}B/K_{0}}\cong S_{0}^{-1}B

by Lemma 3.6, because S0−1​BS_{0}^{-1}B is a smooth K0K_{0}-algebra by Lemma 4.2.

Each element of KK belongs to Frac⁡(S0−1​B)\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}(S_{0}^{-1}B) and is algebraic over K0K_{0}, hence integral over S0−1​BS_{0}^{-1}B; as S0−1​BS_{0}^{-1}B is normal, K⊆S0−1​BK\subseteq S_{0}^{-1}B and hence S0−1​B=RS_{0}^{-1}B=R. We may therefore rewrite (11) as:

(12) ⋀2ΩR/K0≅R.\textstyle\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R/K_{0}}\cong R.

Applying [18, 26.H] to K0⊆K⊆RK_{0}\subseteq K\subseteq R gives the exact sequence of RR-modules

ΩK/K0⊗KR→ΩR/K0→ΩR/K→0,\Omega_{K/K_{0}}\otimes_{K}R\to\Omega_{R/K_{0}}\to\Omega_{R/K}\to 0,

where ΩK/K0=0\Omega_{K/K_{0}}=0 by [18, 27.B]. So ΩR/K≅ΩR/K0\Omega_{R/K}\cong\Omega_{R/K_{0}} and hence (12) gives ⋀2ΩR/K≅R\bigwedge^{2}\Omega_{R/K}\cong R. So R∈𝔇⁡(K)R\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) by Theorem 3.2. ∎

Let 𝐤{\rm\bf k} be a field of characteristic zero, let B∈𝒩⁡(𝐤)B\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}) and consider locally nilpotent derivations D:B→BD:B\to B. See 1.1 for the definition of klnd⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B). It is known that if A∈klnd⁡(B)A\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B) then trdegA⁡(B)=1\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{A}(B)=1, and if A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} are distinct elements of klnd⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B) then trdegA1∩A2⁡(B)≥2\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{A_{1}\cap A_{2}}(B)\geq 2. We are interested in the situation where trdegA1∩A2⁡(B)=2\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{A_{1}\cap A_{2}}(B)=2, i.e., when A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} are distinct and have an intersetion which is as large as possible.

4.4 Corollary.

Let B∈𝒩⁡(𝐤)B\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}), where 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is a field of characteristic zero. If A1,A2∈klnd⁡(B)A_{1},A_{2}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B) are such that trdegA1∩A2⁡(B)=2\operatorname{{\rm trdeg}}_{A_{1}\cap A_{2}}(B)=2, then the following hold.

  1. (a)

    Let R=A1∩A2R=A_{1}\cap A_{2} and K=Frac⁡RK=\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}R. Then K⊗RB∈𝔇⁡(K)K\otimes_{R}B\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K).

  2. (b)

    If BB is a UFD then there exists a finite sequence of local slice constructions which transforms A1A_{1} into A2A_{2}.

Remark.

This generalizes results 1.10 and 1.13 of [6]. Local slice construction was originally defined in [12] in the case B=𝐤[3]B={\rm\bf k}^{[3]}, and was later generalized in [5].

Proof of Corollary 4.4.

Let S=R∖{0}S=R\setminus\{0\}, 𝒜i=S−1​Ai\mathcal{A}_{i}=S^{-1}A_{i} (i=1,2i=1,2) and ℬ=S−1​B=K⊗RB\mathcal{B}=S^{-1}B=K\otimes_{R}B. If Di∈lnd⁡(B)D_{i}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(B) has kernel AiA_{i}, then S−1​Di∈lnd⁡(ℬ)S^{-1}D_{i}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc lnd}}(\mathcal{B}) has kernel 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i}; thus 𝒜1,𝒜2∈klnd⁡(ℬ)\mathcal{A}_{1},\mathcal{A}_{2}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(\mathcal{B}). Using that A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} are factorially closed in BB, we obtain 𝒜1∩𝒜2⊆K\mathcal{A}_{1}\cap\mathcal{A}_{2}\subseteq K, so ML⁡(ℬ)⊆K\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(\mathcal{B})\subseteq K. The reverse inclusion is trivial (K∗⊆ℬ∗⊆ML⁡(ℬ)K^{*}\subseteq\mathcal{B}^{*}\subseteq\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(\mathcal{B})), so ML⁡(ℬ)=K\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(\mathcal{B})=K. Then ℬ∈𝔇⁡(K)\mathcal{B}\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) by Theorem 4.1, so assertion (a) is proved.

In [5, 3.3], one defines a graph klnd ⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}(B) whose vertex-set is klnd⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B); then, given A,A′∈klnd⁡(B)A,A^{\prime}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B), one says that A′A^{\prime} can be obtained from AA “by a local slice construction” if there exists an edge in klnd ⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}(B) joining vertices AA and A′A^{\prime}. So assertion (b) of the Corollary is equivalent to the existence of a path in klnd ⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}(B) going from A1A_{1} to A2A_{2}. Paragraph [5, 3.2.2] also defines a subgraph klnd R⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}_{R}(B) of the graph klnd ⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}(B), and clearly A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} are two vertices of klnd R⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}_{R}(B); so, to prove (b), it suffices to show that klnd R⁡(B)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}_{R}(B) is a connected graph. We have R∈ℛin​(B)R\in\mathcal{R}^{\mbox{\scriptsize in}}(B) (cf. [5, 5.2]) and consequently (cf. [5, 5.3], using that BB is a UFD) we have an isomorphism of graphs klnd R⁡(B)≅klnd K⁡(ℬ)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}_{R}(B)\cong\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}_{K}(\mathcal{B}). As ℬ∈𝔇⁡(K)\mathcal{B}\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K) by part (a), we may apply [5, 4.8] and conclude that klnd K⁡(ℬ)\operatorname{\mbox{\lx@text@underline{\sc klnd}\,}}_{K}(\mathcal{B}) is connected. Assertion (b) is proved. ∎

The following is a trivial consequence of Corollary 4.4.

4.5 Corollary.

Let B∈𝒩⁡(𝐤)B\in\mathcal{N}({\rm\bf k}), where 𝐤{\rm\bf k} is a field of characteristic zero. Suppose that BB has transcendence degree two over ML⁡(B)\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(B).

  1. (1)

    Let R=ML⁡(B)R=\operatorname{{\rm ML}}(B) and K=Frac⁡RK=\operatorname{{\rm Frac}}R. Then K⊗RB∈𝔇⁡(K)K\otimes_{R}B\in\operatorname{{{\mathfrak{D}}}}(K).

  2. (2)

    If BB is a UFD then, for any A1,A2∈klnd⁡(B)A_{1},A_{2}\in\operatorname{\mbox{\sc klnd}}(B), there exists a finite sequence of local slice constructions which transforms A1A_{1} into A2A_{2}.
